Medication Fridge Breakdown Procedure

*Supersedes the version effective 1 April 2025. Escalation changed to also require a call to the supplying pharmacy, not only the on-call manager.*

If the fridge fails

Keep the affected fridge closed, do not move stock on assumption, and call both the on-call manager and the supplying pharmacy (a new requirement — the previous version only required the on-call manager) for advice on whether the stock remains usable; see Immediate containment below for the full response, including when a validated alternative storage location may be used.

Immediate containment

When the medicines-fridge temperature is outside range or the unit fails, staff keep the door closed, note the current and available minimum/maximum readings, label the unit not for use and inform the responsible nurse or manager. Stock is not moved into a domestic refrigerator or discarded on assumption. A validated alternative refrigerator or insulated container is prepared where authorised.

Clinical and pharmacy advice

Staff list every affected medicine, batch where available, storage requirement and estimated exposure time and obtain product-specific pharmacy or manufacturer advice. The decision to use, quarantine or replace each item is recorded. Time-critical doses are escalated so an alternative supply or clinically appropriate plan can be arranged without bypassing prescribing controls.

Recovery and assurance

The failed unit is inspected and must demonstrate a stable compliant temperature before return to service. Quarantined stock remains segregated until a documented decision is made. Temperature records, exposure assessment, advice, stock disposition, engineer report and any omitted-dose or incident record are retained together, and repeated failures trigger equipment replacement review.

Medication Fridge Monitoring: Daily Checks

Purpose and scope

This guidance sets out how the medication fridge is monitored at every Alderbridge site. It applies to every shift storing medication requiring refrigeration.

Policy statement

The medication fridge is checked and logged daily, keeping medication within its required temperature range so that it remains safe and effective for resident use.

Definitions

**Acceptable range** 2 to 8 degrees Celsius, the temperature band medication stored in the fridge must remain within. **Fridge log** the daily record of the fridge's temperature, checked and signed each day. **Out-of-range reading** any reading outside the acceptable range, requiring immediate action.

1. Check and record the fridge temperature once daily, at a consistent time, in the fridge log.
2. Where a reading is out of range, recheck immediately; if confirmed, follow the Medication Fridge Breakdown Procedure without delay.
3. Keep the fridge door closed as much as practicable, avoiding unnecessary or prolonged opening.
4. Report a fridge showing a recurring near-boundary reading to facilities, even if it has not yet gone fully out of range.

Interaction with other Alderbridge policies

This guidance works alongside the Medication Fridge Breakdown Procedure (the response once an out-of-range reading is confirmed) and the Medication Ordering and Stock Policy (governing the medication the fridge holds).

Worked example

A worked example illustrates the daily check in practice. The morning shift lead checks the fridge temperature at the same time each day as part of their routine, records 4 degrees in the log, and moves on; a fortnight later, a reading of 9 degrees prompts an immediate recheck and, once confirmed, the breakdown procedure is followed straight away rather than waiting to see if it corrects itself.

Resident and family involvement in medication decisions

Wherever a resident has capacity, they are involved directly in decisions about their own medication; where capacity is lacking, family or an advocate is involved in a best-interests process rather than a purely clinical decision being made without any input beyond the care team itself.

Medication reconciliation on admission and transfer

Every resident's full medication list is reconciled against the prescribing GP's own record at admission, and again at any hospital transfer in either direction, since a mismatch between what a resident is believed to be taking and what they are actually prescribed is one of the most common sources of a serious medication error. This reconciliation is completed by a registered nurse or the registered manager, never left solely to an informal handover conversation.

Managing a medication change communicated verbally

Where a GP communicates a medication change verbally, this is confirmed in writing before the change is actually implemented, except in a genuine emergency where immediate action is clinically necessary; a verbal instruction alone is not treated as sufficient authority for an ongoing change to a resident's regular medication regimen.

End of life medication considerations

Medication management at the end of a resident's life often involves a different balance of priorities than routine administration, with comfort and symptom control given particular weight consistent with the End of Life Care Policy; this overarching document's core principles still apply in full, adapted to that different clinical context.

Purpose and scope

This guidance explains how staff respond to a power outage at any Alderbridge site. It applies to every shift, including night shifts when fewer staff are on duty.

Policy statement

A power outage is managed calmly, prioritising resident warmth, safety and medication integrity, while the wider Business Continuity Plan Summary is triggered if the outage is prolonged.

Definitions

Supplier and pharmacy relationship management

Where a resident is admitted with their own medication already dispensed, this is checked against the GP or hospital discharge letter, recorded in the electronic ordering system as an opening balance rather than a new order, and either used down before the next pharmacy order or returned to the family if it does not match the current prescription, so that the stock record reflects genuine holdings from the point of admission rather than starting from an assumed zero.

Seasonal and holiday-period ordering

Around a bank holiday or a period when the pharmacy's own delivery schedule is reduced, the senior carer raises the relevant order in the electronic ordering system earlier than the normal weekly cycle to avoid a late Friday order arriving after a reduced-service weekend, since running short over a holiday period is harder to correct quickly than during a normal week.

Purpose and scope

This procedure sets out how staff respond to a suspected gas leak at any Alderbridge site. It applies to every member of staff on shift.

Policy statement

A suspected gas leak is treated as an immediate, serious hazard, evacuated and reported without delay, since gas presents a risk that can escalate very quickly if not acted on immediately.

Evacuate the immediate area on any suspected gas leak, moving residents and staff to a safe distance.

Do not operate a light switch, or any other electrical switch, in the affected area, since a spark can ignite escaping gas.

Purpose and scope

Policy statement

The medication fridge is checked and logged daily, keeping medication within its required temperature range so that it remains safe and effective for resident use.

Resident and family involvement in medication decisions

Wherever a resident has capacity, they are involved directly in decisions about their own medication; where capacity is lacking, family or an advocate is involved in a best-interests process rather than a purely clinical decision being made without any input beyond the care team itself.

Medication reconciliation on admission and transfer

Every resident's full medication list is reconciled against the prescribing GP's own record at admission, and again at any hospital transfer in either direction, since a mismatch between what a resident is believed to be taking and what they are actually prescribed is one of the most common sources of a serious medication error. This reconciliation is completed by a registered nurse or the registered manager, never left solely to an informal handover conversation.

Managing a medication change communicated verbally

Where a GP communicates a medication change verbally, this is confirmed in writing before the change is actually implemented, except in a genuine emergency where immediate action is clinically necessary; a verbal instruction alone is not treated as sufficient authority for an ongoing change to a resident's regular medication regimen.

End of life medication considerations

Medication management at the end of a resident's life often involves a different balance of priorities than routine administration, with comfort and symptom control given particular weight consistent with the End of Life Care Policy; this overarching document's core principles still apply in full, adapted to that different clinical context.

Purpose and scope

This policy sets out how Alderbridge Care Group ensures medication is prescribed, ordered, stored, administered, recorded and reviewed safely and consistently across every site. It applies to every member of staff who has any contact with medication, from a registered nurse administering an injection to a housekeeping colleague who happens to find a dropped tablet on the floor. It does not cover community support workers assisting a person to self-administer under a documented capacity assessment — that specific activity is governed by the Self-Administration of Medication Policy, which this policy defers to entirely rather than duplicating.

Policy statement

Alderbridge Care Group believes that safe medication practice is one of the clearest, most measurable expressions of good care. Errors are treated as a system-level learning opportunity in the first instance, not automatically as individual misconduct, in line with the Medication Error Report Form's own no-blame first-response principle — although a pattern of repeated, avoidable error, or a single deliberately concealed error, is escalated through the Disciplinary Procedure.

Definitions

**MAR chart** the Medication Administration Record on which every dose given, refused, or omitted is signed for at the time of administration, never in advance and never retrospectively without a documented late-entry reason. **PRN medication** medication prescribed to be given only when required, subject to its own written PRN protocol describing the specific circumstances, maximum frequency and maximum daily dose. **Homely remedy** a limited over-the-counter remedy that may be given without an individual prescription, governed separately by the Homely Remedies Policy. **Competency assessment** the observed, signed-off assessment confirming a named member of staff is safe to administer medication unsupervised, distinct from simply having attended training. **Controlled drug** a medication subject to the additional legal controls and double-signing requirements set out separately in the Controlled Drugs Procedure.

Historical development of the medication suite

The medication policy suite has grown incrementally since Alderbridge's founding, beginning with a single combined medication policy that, as the organisation grew and guidance itself became more specific, was gradually separated into the distinct specific policies this overarching document now signposts.

Interfacing with an external pharmacy provider

Alderbridge's contracted pharmacy providers are bound by a service level agreement referencing this overarching policy and its suite, ensuring an external pharmacy's own processes align with Alderbridge's internal standards.

Escalation contacts summary across the suite

Situation First contact Second contact if unresolved
--- --- ---
Medication error or near miss Registered nurse or senior carer on duty Registered manager
Fridge temperature out of range Senior carer on duty Facilities and Medication Fridge Breakdown Procedure
Suspected covert administration need GP and registered nurse Multidisciplinary team best-interests meeting
Medication-related safeguarding concern Safeguarding Lead directly Registered manager

Resident and family involvement in medication decisions

Wherever a resident has capacity, they are involved directly in decisions about their own medication; where capacity is lacking, family or an advocate is involved in a best-interests process rather than a purely clinical decision being made without any input beyond the care team itself.

Medication reconciliation on admission and transfer

Every resident's full medication list is reconciled against the prescribing GP's own record at admission, and again at any hospital transfer in either direction, since a mismatch between what a resident is believed to be taking and what they are actually prescribed is one of the most common sources of a serious medication error. This reconciliation is completed by a registered nurse or the registered manager, never left solely to an informal handover conversation.

Managing a medication change communicated verbally

Where a GP communicates a medication change verbally, this is confirmed in writing before the change is actually implemented, except in a genuine emergency where immediate action is clinically necessary; a verbal instruction alone is not treated as sufficient authority for an ongoing change to a resident's regular medication regimen.

End of life medication considerations

Medication management at the end of a resident's life often involves a different balance of priorities than routine administration, with comfort and symptom control given particular weight consistent with the End of Life Care Policy; this overarching document's core principles still apply in full, adapted to that different clinical context.

the escalation point. Power is lost during a storm at 9pm. Emergency lighting activates as expected, and the shift lead monitors the situation; when power is not restored after 30 minutes, they contact the on-call registered manager as required, who begins assessing whether the full continuity plan should be triggered.

Frequently asked questions

**Should the medication fridge be opened to check on medication during a short outage?** No, keeping it closed preserves its temperature for several hours; it is only checked once power is confirmed restored, or if the outage becomes prolonged. **Who decides when to call the emergency generator supplier, where a site has one?** The on-call registered manager, once the 30-minute threshold is reached.

Training and competency

All staff are shown the emergency lighting locations and the 30-minute escalation point during induction.

Communicating with residents and families

Residents are reassured calmly and kept informed in simple terms about what is happening, and a family member who contacts the site during a known outage is told honestly what is known, including the escalation status, rather than given a vague or overly reassuring answer that does not match the actual situation.

Closing note

A calm, practised response to a power outage keeps residents safe and reassured, and this guidance exists to make that calm response automatic rather than improvised.
